slides.title: Case Management Training — Day 1
slides.notes: Welcome to Day 1 of Case Management Training with Legal Support Help. All week we work one file, John Doe versus Robert Smith, a passenger injury from a collision on February 6th, 2026. Today we open that file. We look at what a Case Manager actually owns, how a case moves from the first call to resolution, and how you keep it clean, compliant and on time. Keep John's file in mind as we go, because every idea on these slides lands on it.

slides.title: Training Agenda
slides.notes: Today has three parts. First, the fundamentals: what case management is and what you are responsible for. Second, intake, case evaluation and the decision to accept John Doe's case, including the conflict check and the coverage behind the claim. Third, the Treatment Phase, where most of a personal injury case's value is built or lost. On our file, that is where the fourteen-day gap sits, so pay close attention there.

slides.title: What is Case Management?
slides.notes: Case management is the coordination, tracking and handling of a case from intake to resolution. The slide gives three tests, and every task on a file should pass all of them. Timely progression means nothing sits without a next step and a date. Documentation and compliance means that if it isn't in the file, it didn't happen. And communication means the client, Atty. Thorne, the carriers and the providers each know what they need, when they need it. On John's file, those parties are already lining up: Keystone, Harbor Point, Cardinal State, Peach State, and a growing list of providers. Your job is to keep all of them moving in step.

slides.title: The General Process
slides.notes: These seven stages are the life of a file, from intake and opening through planning, documentation, communication, monitoring, billing support, and finally resolution and closing. The point of the arrows is that nothing gets skipped. A file that jumps from intake straight to treatment, without a plan or a coverage picture, will stall later. John Doe's file opened with the intake call on February 9th, 2026, and it will travel through every one of these stages this week. Atty. Thorne makes the legal decisions along the way, but you are the one constant who carries the file from start to finish.

slides.title: Key Duties
slides.notes: Here are the duties that fill a Case Manager's day. Notice how practical they are. Case updates and summaries keep Atty. Thorne current without him reading every page. Compliance monitoring means you know every deadline, starting with the statute of limitations, docketed on our file for February 6th, 2028. Case health analysis means reading the whole file for risk, the way you would spot John's fourteen-day gap on day one. And the last duty matters most. You plan and you recommend. Decisions of legal strategy, value and settlement belong to the attorney.

slides.title: Understanding Case Phases
slides.notes: A case moves through structured phases, and each one has its own goals and deliverables. Intake; investigation, which we also call claim set up; treatment; pre-demand; demand; settlement and lien negotiation; disbursement; and litigation when a case doesn't settle. Knowing the phase tells you what the file needs next. Today we cover the first three. On John's file, that runs from the intake call on February 9th, 2026, through claim set up with the carriers, and into his treatment, which ends when Dr. Reyes declares maximum medical improvement on June 12th, 2026.

slides.title: Case Phase: Intake
slides.notes: Intake is where you take control of the file, and it is much more than data entry. Everything later depends on it. A wrong date of loss, a missed party or a skipped conflict check will follow the case all the way to the demand. The slide lists four jobs: capture complete client details, screen for conflicts, assess whether the case is viable, and build a properly structured file. On our file, that means John Doe's date of birth, August 14th, 1991, his address at 2214 Maple Hollow Road in Riverton, his phone and email, the date of loss, and the fact that he was a passenger. This is also the phase that decides whether the case moves forward at all.

slides.title: Intake in Practice
slides.notes: Here is intake as a real workflow. You talk with the client or review what they sent. You ask the structured questions: who, what, when, where and how. You run the conflict check before anything else moves. You review the documents, and you build the file with the firm's naming convention. On our file, the intake call was Monday, February 9th, 2026, and John signed the retainer and the HIPAA authorization in the office the same day. The file number is L S H 2026 M V A 770412. The conflict check covers every name on the file, not only the defendant: Robert Smith, Keystone Mutual, the host driver Kevin Alvarez, and John's mother, Margaret Doe. Then the case is approved or escalated, and the file is logged. You should be able to run that sequence on your own and tell the client clearly what happens next.

slides.title: Intake and Initial Client Contact
slides.notes: Initial client contact gathers the basic facts, judges urgency, and decides whether the case can go forward. Your role as Case Manager starts once intake is done. You are the quality check before a case becomes active. Read the intake the way an adjuster eventually will. On John's file, one fact should stop you at once: the crash was February 6th, and he had not yet been treated when he called on the 9th. His first treatment didn't come until February 20th. That fourteen-day gap is flagged at intake, not discovered at the demand. Being the gatekeeper means you catch it, document it, and make sure Atty. Thorne knows.

slides.title: Case Acceptance Determination
slides.notes: After the verification call confirms the facts of loss, the question changes. You are no longer gathering information. You are checking whether the case meets the firm's criteria for acceptance, based on verified facts and a complete intake. On our file, the facts hold up: John was a restrained front-seat passenger, the Riverton police report cites Robert Smith for failure to stop, and there is a recovery stack of insurance behind the claim. The risk is also clear: the treatment gap. The Case Manager presents both sides in the file, and Atty. Thorne makes the acceptance decision.

slides.title: Common Intake Bottlenecks
slides.notes: Intake bottlenecks are the places where a file slows down, gets stuck or goes inconsistent. The slide names five common causes: missing information, slow client responses, poorly documented submissions, delays in verification or the conflict check, and unclear eligibility decisions. They matter because every day lost at intake is a day lost against the statute of limitations, and a day the client may go untreated. Over the next few slides we take each one in turn, and see where it shows up on John Doe's file.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Incomplete Client Information
slides.notes: The first bottleneck is incomplete information: missing contact details or incident facts, no supporting documents, or a vague case summary. Each one sends you back to the client before the file can move. On our file, some blanks are normal on day one. Cardinal State hasn't assigned an adjuster yet, and Keystone gave its $10,000 limit verbally but won't confirm it in writing until it has signed authorizations. You record exactly what is known and what is pending, and you set a follow-up for each gap, so nothing stays blank by accident.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Delayed Client Follow-Up
slides.notes: The second bottleneck is the client who goes quiet. Clarification requests go unanswered, confirmations never come back, documents trickle in. John Doe's file shows this in its first week. The last logged contact was February 10th, 2026. Calls followed on the 11th, the 13th and the 16th, then written warnings, and a call to his mother, Margaret, as the emergency contact, with no case details shared. One lesson from the file: the first two voicemails were left but never logged, and the system flagged it. An attempt you don't log is an attempt you can't prove. John finally called back on February 23rd, after the Final Warning Letter went out.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Conflict Check Delays
slides.notes: The third bottleneck is the conflict check: system backlogs, incomplete entries, or unclear information about the other side. The rule is simple. The conflict check runs before anything else moves, and it runs on complete names. On our file, the defendant is Robert Smith, with an address on the police report of 118 Larkspur Lane, Riverton. But the check also covers the carriers and the people around the claim, including Kevin Alvarez, the host driver, and Margaret Doe. A conflict check run on half the information is not a conflict check.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Intake Form Errors
slides.notes: The fourth bottleneck is the intake form error: wrong dates, inconsistent statements, missing signatures or authorizations, and duplicate or misfiled records. These are cheap to fix at intake and expensive to fix later. Our file proves it. Months later, Summit Imaging's MRI history gave the injury date as February 16th instead of February 6th, and it took a written correction request to fix it. So at intake, confirm the date of loss, February 6th, 2026, against the police report, and make sure the retainer and the HIPAA authorization are both signed and filed.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Case Eligibility Uncertainty
slides.notes: The fifth bottleneck is eligibility uncertainty: an intake with no clear legal assessment, a case that needs attorney review, or facts of loss or liability that are ambiguous. When eligibility is unclear, don't guess and don't sit on it. Escalate the file to the attorney and document why. On John's file, liability looks strong, but the fourteen-day gap is a real question for value. That isn't yours to settle. Write it down plainly, attach what supports it, and let Atty. Thorne decide.

slides.title: Tools for Case Planning
slides.notes: In a legal setting, case management moves from best effort to strict compliance, and your tools make that possible: the case management system, task trackers and calendars, document management and workflow automation. The strategy behind them is simple. Every case is a race against the statute of limitations and against the gap in treatment defense. On John's file, both are already on the board: the SOL docketed for February 6th, 2028, and a fourteen-day gap. In intake and investigation the focus is liability and coverage. Here that means Harbor Point's P I P on the Escape, the BI and both UM layers, and the police report, R P D 26 018842. It also means preserving Margaret's doorbell video, which John was told to keep on February 17th. In treatment the focus is damages: compliance, no further gaps, and early imaging, which for John was the cervical MRI at Summit Imaging on March 13th. In the demand phase it is value: the specials and a final narrative. And in litigation, it is evidence: discovery, depositions and experts.

slides.title: Bottleneck: Communication Gaps
slides.notes: The last bottleneck is the communication gap: intake not updating the Case Manager, a packet that arrives incomplete, or departments talking past each other. On a file like John's, many hands touch it early: the intake team, the carriers, the clinic, Atty. Thorne. Closing the gaps is part of your job. Confirm you have the complete intake packet, log every hand-off with the date and the person, and if something is missing, ask for it the same day rather than waiting for it to surface.

slides.title: Claim Set Up: Coverage and Liability
slides.notes: Now claim set up, the early evaluation. It rests on two questions. Coverage: which policies apply, what type, what limits, and what exclusions. Liability: who caused the crash, whether fault is clear, shared or disputed, what evidence proves it, and whether comparative negligence comes into play. On our file, coverage takes real work, because John was a passenger and owns no car, so no policy of his own applies. Liability looks clean, but you still ask the comparative negligence question. The EMS run report records him as a restrained front-seat passenger, and you keep that record, because the defense may later argue the opposite.

slides.title: Case Projection
slides.notes: Case projection is the early estimate of value, risk and how the case will move. It draws on coverage, liability strength, injury severity, expected treatment and documentation quality. Each piece answers a question. Coverage asks whether there is money to pay. Liability asks who is responsible. Projection asks what the case is likely worth and how it will move. On John's file, the coverage ceiling is a $40,000 stack, liability is strong, and the fourteen-day gap is the obvious risk to value. Remember that value is Atty. Thorne's call. Your projection supports his decision; it is never a promise to the client.

slides.title: Case Example: Coverage Analysis
slides.notes: Now let's apply this to John Doe versus Robert Smith. John was the front-seat passenger in Kevin Alvarez's 2020 Ford Escape. Robert Smith, driving a 2017 Chevrolet Silverado, ran the all-way stop at Maple Hollow Road and Birch Avenue and struck the passenger door on February 6th, 2026, at about 7:10 in the morning. The coverage stack pays in order. First, Smith's BI with Keystone Mutual, claim K M 26 440871, a $10,000 limit, which Keystone gave verbally and you confirm in writing. Second, Host UM with Harbor Point, the Escape's policy, $20,000, which opens only once the BI is exhausted. Third, Relative UM with Cardinal State Mutual, $10,000, because John lives with his mother, Margaret Doe. That is a $40,000 stack. Margaret's Bluewater policy rejected UM in writing, so it adds no layer. The key insight: never settle or release the BI claim without the UM carriers' written consent, because doing so can forfeit the stack.

slides.title: Case Example: Liability Determination
slides.notes: Now liability. This was a side-impact collision at an all-way stop in Riverton. Kevin Alvarez stopped eastbound on Maple Hollow Road and proceeded. Robert Smith, northbound on Birch Avenue, didn't stop, and hit the front passenger door at about 28 miles per hour, pushing the Escape into Margaret's parked Civic. The evidence is unusually good: the Riverton police report, R P D 26 018842, citing Smith for failure to stop; an independent witness, Ruth Calloway, of 2209 Maple Hollow Road; and Margaret's doorbell-camera video. John was a passenger, so none of the driving was his. Your job is to check each piece against the police report and make sure the video is preserved before it is overwritten. And remember, fault and value are Atty. Thorne's call. You document the facts; you never predict the outcome.

slides.title: Case Planning Framework: Regulatory Triple-Check
slides.notes: Before clinical planning begins, clear the Regulatory Triple-Check. First, HIPAA. A general release isn't enough; you need a claim-specific authorization that names the date of loss and lets you talk with the legal and insurance parties. John signed his at intake on February 9th, 2026. Second, Medicare and Medicaid reporting. If the client is 65 or older or on SSDI, the case is reported to the BCRC under the MMSEA, or the settlement can freeze. John is thirty-four and working, but you confirm it and document it; you never assume. Third, subrogation and payer order. On our file, Harbor Point's P I P pays first, then Harbor Point's MedPay, then Peach State Health Plan, which asserted its reimbursement right on first notice, then the Letter of Protection with Riverton Spine and Rehab.

slides.title: The Three-Pillar Case Plan
slides.notes: The case plan is often due within 30 to 60 days, depending on the state, and it stands on three pillars. Clinical covers the interventions. For John, that is chiropractic and physical therapy at Riverton Spine and Rehab, two to three visits a week for twelve weeks, and an orthopedic consult with Dr. Alana Reyes at Lakeside Orthopedics. Functional covers daily life and work. John is a warehouse shift lead at Northgate Distribution, lifting up to 50 pounds and driving a forklift, so his return to work status matters. And subrogation is the payer order we just covered. The fourteen-day gap also goes into the plan's risks band, written down plainly from the start.

slides.title: Mandatory Disclosure & Compliance Tracking
slides.notes: Your file is discoverable in litigation, so keep it clean. Three things to track. Record integrity: your system should be SOC2 compliant, with an audit trail no one can alter. State-specific timelines: in no-fault states like New York or Florida, the plan must schedule independent medical exams. That is the general rule. Riverton is an add-on P I P state, not no-fault, but it does have an Emergency Medical Condition rule: without a physician's finding, P I P medical benefits stop at $2,500. So know which rules your file actually runs under. And Letter of Protection management. John has Peach State coverage, but Riverton Spine and Rehab is out of network, so his care there runs under an LOP signed February 23rd, 2026. Track every visit and every charge on it, so no bill surprises anyone at the end.

slides.title: The Golden Rule of US Claim Set-Up
slides.notes: The golden rule of claim set up is coordinate, don't commingle. The medical plan and the legal claim run on two parallel tracks that never cross. Never write a legal opinion into a medical note, because defense counsel will use it to attack your neutrality. On John's file, a note that says the client attended his Riverton Spine and Rehab visit and reported neck pain is a fact. A note that says the gap won't hurt the case is an opinion, and it doesn't belong there. Keep your file clean, because everything in it can be discovered.

slides.title: The Treatment Phase: Core Objectives
slides.notes: Now the Treatment Phase. The question changes from what does the client need, to is the plan working. Your role rests on three pillars. Facilitation means the client can actually reach care: transportation, paperwork and scheduling. Coordination means the chiropractor, the therapist and the doctor aren't working at cross-purposes. Advocacy means stepping in when the client hits a wall. On John's file, all three are tested. He has no car of his own, he is seeing several providers at once, and his care is paid from several sources. This phase is the engine room of the case, and you balance support, monitoring and problem-solving throughout.

slides.title: Key Responsibilities & Skills
slides.notes: Your responsibilities here come in three parts. Monitoring progress means looking at real clinical and functional outcomes, not checking boxes. At a check-in, ask whether John made his Tuesday visit and whether the numbness in his right hand has changed, not just how he's feeling. Then document in GIRP or SOAP format. Identifying barriers means being a detective. Internal barriers include motivation and mental health; external ones include transportation and insurance problems. And crisis intervention means that when something urgent comes up, you deal with it first, and adjust the plan around it.

slides.title: Essential Client Communication Strategies
slides.notes: Three communication skills keep a client on track. Motivational interviewing keeps commitment going after the newness of treatment wears off. Boundaries protect you from burnout and keep the client moving toward self-sufficiency. Active listening makes the client feel heard and reduces misunderstandings with providers. And remember, treatment is a cycle, not a straight line. Assess the response, evaluate the plan, and adjust. On John's file, the plan changes more than once: Dr. Reyes orders an MRI, then refers him to pain management, then counseling is added. When a client isn't reaching their goals, look at the plan first, not the person.

slides.title: Handling the Treatment Phase: Documentation
slides.notes: Your notes are the legal and professional record of treatment, so structure them with GIRP. Goal: which part of the plan are we working on today. Intervention: what you did. Response: how the client reacted, in his own words where you can. Plan: the next step and its date. Midway through treatment, many clients plateau as the early energy fades. That's where motivational interviewing helps. Develop discrepancy, by showing the gap between what the client is doing and what he wants, such as John getting back to full duty at Northgate. Roll with resistance: don't argue; explore why. And use OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening and summaries.

slides.title: Handling the Treatment Phase: Coordination & Boundaries
slides.notes: You are the hub of the wheel, and the key skill is the warm handoff. Instead of handing a client a phone number, you say: let's call them together and book it now. That stops the referral leak, where clients drop out between providers. On John's file there are several transitions: from urgent care to the emergency department at Riverton General, then to Riverton Spine and Rehab, Lakeside Orthopedics, Summit Imaging and Crescent Pain and Spine. Each is a point where he could slip. Then manage boundaries and avoid mission creep, where every new problem pulls you off the main goal. Coach the client rather than solving everything yourself. And end every contact with one question: what is the one thing that might get in the way this week?

slides.title: Red Flags: Physical Therapy & Surgery
slides.notes: Know the standard treatment protocols and their red flags. Physical therapy is usually the baseline of care. Red flags are more than twelve sessions with no improvement and no referral or imaging, passive care with no active exercise, and two or more missed appointments, which lets the defense argue the injury isn't serious. On our file, that last one is real. In April, John missed visits on the 3rd, the 7th, the 9th and the 14th, and you need to know why. For surgery, the red flags are about safety: surgery before therapy or injections outside an emergency, left and right switched in the records, a fever or redness the client is told to ignore, and sharp mechanical pain after surgery. John's file has no surgery; his care stayed conservative, with one epidural steroid injection.

slides.title: Red Flags: Pain Management & Behavioral Health
slides.notes: Pain management is the most scrutinized area, because of opioid rules and medical necessity audits. The red flags on the slide are general: an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative prescribed together; a urine drug screen showing the client isn't taking his medication; and doses rising with no change in diagnosis. On John's file, pain management means Dr. Omar Haddad at Crescent Pain and Spine, who gave a cervical epidural steroid injection on May 15th, 2026. Traumatic brain injury isn't part of this file, but the red flag is worth knowing: symptoms that never appeared at the E R and then show up months later need medical validation right away. And behavioral health has to be tied to the trauma of the accident. John's counseling was about crash-related anxiety, which is exactly the kind of record that holds up.

slides.title: Case Planning: The Assessment Phase
slides.notes: Before you build a treatment plan, you assess the whole person. Clinical: the physical, cognitive and psychological impairments. Social: housing, family support and money. John lives with his mother, Margaret, and owns no car, which matters for getting to appointments. Pre-morbid status: the baseline before the accident. John had three chiropractic visits in 2021 for low-back stiffness, which resolved, and no prior neck complaints. You find that history before the defense does. And vocational: can he go back to his job? John is a warehouse shift lead at Northgate, who started on January 12th, 2026, at $22 an hour.

slides.title: SMART Goal Setting
slides.notes: In a personal injury case, goals have to be defensible and measurable for clinicians and adjusters alike. Use SMART goals. The slide's example, walking 50 meters with a rolling walker, is general. For John, a specific goal is tied to his job, such as lifting 50 pounds at work again. Measurable means a standardized scale, such as a disability score or the PHQ-9 for mood. Achievable means realistic for the prognosis. Relevant means tied to the neck injury in the claim. And time-bound means a clear milestone, such as the twelve-week review in his plan of care at Riverton Spine and Rehab.

slides.title: The Care Coordination Strategy
slides.notes: The care coordination strategy maps the interventions the client needs, in four groups. Acute and restorative care: surgery, physiotherapy and occupational therapy. On John's file, that's chiropractic and physical therapy, orthopedic care with Dr. Reyes, and the injection at Crescent. Psychological support: counseling for anxiety or trauma. For John, that came through Northgate's employee assistance program, six sessions with Renee Castillo at Stonebridge E A P Services. Durable medical equipment: wheelchairs, ramps and assistive technology, which John's file doesn't call for. And rehabilitation milestones: the steps from one level of care to the next.

slides.title: The Standard Treatment Map
slides.notes: This is the Standard Treatment Map, the typical path of care in a personal injury case: emergency services and the E R, then imaging, then providers like chiropractic, physical therapy and orthopedics, then pain management, and, where needed, surgery and post-operative care. The map is general. Now trace John's path on it. EMS saw him at the scene and he declined transport. His first treatment was Riverton Urgent Care on February 20th, and from there an ambulance took him to Riverton General Hospital's emergency department, where he was kept overnight. Then Riverton Spine and Rehab from February 24th, Lakeside Orthopedics on March 5th, the MRI at Summit Imaging on March 13th, and pain management at Crescent in May. Learning the map lets you see when a client drifts off it.

slides.title: Treatment Road Map Mastery
slides.notes: Mastering the map is the difference between watching a recovery and driving it, because departures from the map are what trigger insurance denials and independent medical exams. Phase one, acute, days 1 to 14: the E R, imaging and early care, with your focus on causation and P I P or MedPay coverage. On John's file, those fourteen days passed with no treatment at all, which is why the gap is so important. Phase two, sub-acute, weeks 2 to 8: active therapy two or three times a week and specialist follow-up. Phase three, restorative, months 2 to 6: injections and psychological adjustment, like John's injection in May and his counseling. Phase four, maintenance, ends with maximum medical improvement, which Dr. Reyes declared on June 12th, 2026.

slides.title: Variance Analysis: Why the Map Fails
slides.notes: When a client drifts off the map, find out why before the insurer stops paying. There are three kinds of variance. Clinical variance is a new complication, like nerve symptoms that weren't in the first report. John's urgent-care note records numbness to his right hand since February 18th, and the MRI later showed a C5-C6 disc herniation. Psychosocial variance covers yellow flags like fear, low mood or no transportation. On our file, that is the crash-related anxiety behind his missed visits in April. And systemic variance is delay in the system itself, such as waiting on an authorization for imaging or a referral.

slides.title: Communication Loops: The Stakeholder Triad
slides.notes: You are the router for information, and a break in any of these three loops can stall a case for months. The clinical loop: the therapist's notes should line up with the orthopedist's orders. For John, Riverton Spine and Rehab's notes should match what Dr. Reyes is seeing. The legal loop: your status reports to Atty. Thorne translate medical terms into what John can't do in daily life, such as lifting at work or playing pickup basketball, because that is the evidence for pain and suffering. And the financial loop: keep the carriers current. On our file, Harbor Point's P I P went to the emergency care, and its MedPay then paid the urgent care, orthopedic and M R I bills until its $5,000 was used up, so you track both ledgers closely.

slides.title: The Golden Standard: Reasonable and Necessary
slides.notes: Every item in your monitoring plan has to meet two tests in utilization review. Reasonable: is this treatment common for this mechanism of injury? Necessary: is there objective evidence, not just reported pain, that it is improving function? Then the red flag rule. The slide uses the Oswestry Disability Index after twelve weeks of therapy as its example, and that is general. On John's file, the same idea shows up when Dr. Reyes, at his March 27th follow-up, refers him on to pain management instead of continuing the same care. A proactive Case Manager looks for the next step, and doesn't let treatment run on when it isn't working.

slides.title: Immediate Action Protocol: A-C-T
slides.notes: When you spot a red flag, use A-C-T. Assess: is this a medical danger, like a fever or hardware failure, or a legal danger, like a gap in care or generic notes? Clarify: call the provider's office and ask directly. Track: document the red flag and what you did about it. On John's file, A-C-T runs in April. On April 8th, Riverton Spine and Rehab sent a missed-visit alert. The Case Manager reviewed the file, then called and texted John the same morning, logging each attempt. If the attorney ever has to make a decision about the case or a provider, your record is the reason he can.

slides.title: Illustration: The Clinical Pathway Flowchart
slides.notes: This flowchart puts the treatment map on one page. Phase one: early diagnostics, establishing causation and the mechanism of injury, and verifying P I P. On John's file, that is the EMS run report noting neck stiffness on the day of the crash, and Harbor Point's P I P, opened February 24th. Phase two: conservative care and imaging. Then the key question: is the patient improving? If not, the variance loop begins, with injections, a specialist referral and psychological screening. John's file went through all three: Crescent, pain management and counseling. Phase three is restorative, and phase four is maximum medical improvement and discharge, where the permanent impairment rating and the final lien resolution set up the settlement.

slides.title: Using the Map for Course Correction
slides.notes: Here is how to use the map for course correction. First, find the plateau with the six-week rule. Adjusters look for a functional change around week six, typically a 20 to 30 percent gain in range of motion or a drop in pain. If the client is still at 10 out of 10 pain after twelve sessions, pivot now; don't wait for a denial. On John's file, his week-six re-evaluation at Riverton Spine and Rehab was scheduled for April 7th, and he missed it, which is itself a warning. Second, measure with objective tools: a disability score every 30 days, gait analysis for leg injuries, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 when progress stalls, and a functional capacity evaluation before a return to work.

slides.title: The Yellow Flag Warning System
slides.notes: Watch for yellow flags, the psychosocial barriers that knock a client off the map: catastrophizing, litigation stress, and dependence on passive care or medication. On John's file, the yellow flag was crash-related anxiety. After April 2nd he avoided riding in cars to appointments, and Dr. Reyes documented anxiety and avoidance on April 20th and referred him for counseling. When you report to the attorney or a carrier, use the map to justify the plan. The slide's example, recommending an MRI and a neurosurgical consult for radicular pain, is general. For John, the MRI was ordered by Dr. Reyes on March 5th. That keeps the treatment reasonable and necessary.

slides.title: Handling Treatment Gaps
slides.notes: Treatment gaps weaken the credibility of the injury, slow recovery, create inconsistent records, and reduce settlement value. Step in early, because a gap explained now is far easier than one explained at the demand. The common causes are missed appointments, transportation, cost and co-pays, work schedules, stopping after temporary relief, and delays in referrals or authorizations. John's file has two gaps. The first is fourteen days, from the crash on February 6th to his first treatment on February 20th. The second is nineteen days of disrupted care in April, from his visit on April 2nd until care resumed on April 21st.

slides.title: Treatment Gaps: Case Manager Responsibilities
slides.notes: Your responsibilities with treatment gaps are concrete. Monitor frequency and attendance. Follow up immediately after a missed visit. Explain to the client why steady treatment matters. Help with transportation, scheduling and referrals. Talk with providers about interruptions. And document every explanation and every follow-up. As best practice, keep the treatment timelines current, and escalate a long or unexplained gap to supervising staff or the attorney. On John's file, that work is visible. After the April missed-visit alert came the calls, texts, an email, a call to Margaret as the emergency contact, and then escalation to Atty. Thorne. John called back on April 17th, and with his consent, evening therapy visits were booked from April 21st. That record is what later protects the value of the case.

slides.title: Bottlenecks: The Escalation Protocol
slides.notes: When a bottleneck stalls care, escalate in three levels. Level one, clinical: contact the provider's office manager, on our file Tammy Greer at Riverton Spine and Rehab, to move notes along or ask for a peer-to-peer review. Level two, administrative: send a notice of delay to the adjuster and the plaintiff's attorney, documenting the barrier to care. Level three, legal: ask the attorney about a motion, or about using a Letter of Protection to get past insurance stalling. That decision always belongs to the attorney. And not every LOP request is accepted: when Summit Imaging asked for one, it was declined, because MedPay applied first.

slides.title: Resolve: The Escalation Ladder
slides.notes: When the map hits a wall, climb the ladder one step at a time. Step A, the clinician: ask for a peer-to-peer review between the treating doctor and the insurer's medical director. Step B, the adjuster: send a status update that says plainly that the delay is raising the total claim cost by extending the period of disability. Step C, the attorney: if step B fails, tell the attorney, who may send a 30-day demand or move the provider to a Letter of Protection. On John's file, Atty. Thorne is the one who makes that call. Your job is to bring him a clean record of each step you took.

slides.title: Thank You!
slides.notes: That completes Day 1. You've seen what a Case Manager owns, how to run a clean intake and acceptance decision, how to set up the claim and its coverage, and how to keep treatment on track. You've also seen John Doe versus Robert Smith from the first call to maximum medical improvement, with its two gaps clearly documented. Next, we take that file into the pre-demand audit and the demand. Thank you for your attention, and bring your questions to the next session.
